notes.1a: The species electrostatically attracted to one another in ionic bonds was described by many candidates. Knowledge of the species involved in a covalent bond was less well known. Only a small minority of candidates described the attraction between two nuclei and a shared pair of electrons.
notes.1b: Use of relative atomic mass rather than proton number for the elements was the most common error. Correct application of the relationship between the number of protons and the number of electrons in these different ions was often seen.
notes.1i: Some excellent diagrams for this mechanism were produced, curly arrows were clearly positioned to show the transfer of a pair of electrons, either in a bond or from a lone pair of electrons when a specific bond is broken or made.
notes.1ii: Clear understanding of the term tertiary bromoalkane was seen in answers which focused on the presence of three different alkyl groups bonded to a carbon atom which is covalently bonded to the bromine atom. Some responses were imprecise, for example ‘when a halogenoalkane is attached to three alkyl groups’. There was also inappropriate use of the term ‘compound’ instead of ‘alkyl group’ and ‘is surrounded by’ instead of ‘is bonded to’.
notes.1iii: Many candidates did not appreciate that, under the conditions described, an alkene rather than an alcohol would be made. Of those who attempted to represent M as an alkene some represented the structure of prop-1-ene or showed a structure with an incorrect number of hydrogen atoms present on the correct carbon skeleton.
notes.2a: The bonding in the Period 3 chlorides was generally well known. A common incorrect answer described SiCl as a giant structure. The majority knew the oxidation states of the Period 3 chlorides stated in the syllabus and correctly deduced the oxidation numbers of PCl and SCl .
notes.2b: Equations which represented the dissolving of sodium chloride were uncommon; many answers described the production of hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide. The formation of H PO on addition of PCl to water was seen more frequently. Equations were not always balanced. Incorrect state symbols for at least one of the species was relatively common.
notes.2i: Clear labelled diagrams which described the presence of cations surrounded by delocalised electrons were seen. Many diagrams were not labelled appropriately.
notes.2ii: Answers regularly gave the correct identification of the structure and bonding present. Explanations observations. Reference to a low melting point for bismuth chloride was seen more regularly than identification of a hydrolysis reaction when it was added to water.
notes.2d: This question was generally well answered. Common errors involved inappropriate unit conversion and incorrect relationships between mass and mol. Sometimes the formula of the chloride deduced from the molecular mass calculated was not a Period 3 chloride.
notes.3i: Identification of the alkene or C=C functional group present in E, with appropriate reference to a specific absorption in its infrared spectrum was relatively common.
notes.3ii: Identification of F with a hydroxyl functional group and appropriate reference to a specific absorption in its infrared spectrum was seen less often. Some answers did not refer to the spectrum and gave an explanation in terms of the formation of a diol on addition of cold dilute acidified KMnO .

notes.3d: Different methods were used to describe the synthesis of C2 from A1 in a multi-step process. Many answers were incomplete. notes.general_comments: General comments This examination paper provided a difficult challenge to the candidates. The highest score achieved by one of the low number of candidates was 31 marks out of 40, this was a very good performance. The statistics for individual questions suggest that candidates had sufficient time to complete the paper. The mean mark was 14 / 40, the median mark was 13 / 40. The four modes were 9, 10, 12 and 13 / 40. As these modal values suggest, the majority of candidates scored between 9 and 13 marks. Very few questions can be said to have been found to be easier, however 40 per cent or more of candidates chose the correct response to each of Questions 2, 5, 7, 12, 13, 17, 19, 20, 22, 26, 27, 30, 31 and 36.
